The two types of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) regarding suffering refer to the observation of that aforementioned suchness immediately following the stage of receptivity (*kṣānti*).
It is the realization of liberation from the afflictions previously abandoned.
Third is the subsequent-knowledge-acceptance regarding suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*),
which refers to the arising of untainted wisdom immediately following that knowledge.
The patience and knowledge regarding the dharma are each individually realized within;
it is said that all subsequent noble dharmas are of this same category.
Fourth is the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*).
This means that immediately following this, untainted knowledge arises,
which definitively confirms and validates the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*).
This is the explanation.
"Suffering" refers to the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
"Dharma" refers to the superior teaching that arises from that truth of suffering.
"Knowledge" refers to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering within the path of preparation;
"patience" refers to...
This refers to the untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) that arises as direct realization within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
Second, the "Dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkhadharmajñāna*) is that which arises immediately after the forbearance (*kṣānti*);
it arises subsequent to the preceding forbearance and takes suchness (*tathatā*) as its object.
It is called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*).
The rest may be fully understood by analogy. Since this is the case for the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), so it is for the others as well.
The remaining three truths each likewise have four aspects;
they are explained according to the truth of suffering.
Furthermore, these constitute sixteen [aspects].
Eighth, observing true suchness (*tathatā*).
Eighth, observing correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*).
Through the patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), one takes suchness as the object of cognition.
Following the pattern of the patience of the subsequent category (*anvaya-kṣānti*) and the subsequent category of knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), one takes knowledge as the object.
Next, regarding the specific cultivation during the stage of practice (*bhāvanā-avasthā*),
one cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path among the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
The *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states:
"Because it is established within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
It further states:
First is the factor of discernment,
which refers to right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Although this is mundane, it...
And after emerging from the supramundane state,
one attains [realization] by means of being able to discern what was personally realized during the stage of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
This intention is explained as follows:
The essence of this right view is subsequently attained wisdom;
therefore, it is called "worldly," yet it is not tainted.
It is called the "world" (*loka*).
Since it is called the world,
it is further stated that it is realized through the analytical vision of the path (*darśanamārga*).
Therefore, one knows that the path of cultivation consists of cultivating the Eightfold Noble Path;
furthermore, within the stage of cultivation, the ten bhūmis are distinct.
Generally speaking:
On each stage, one cultivates all ten pāramitās; however,
according to the specific explanation of the ten stages,
one cultivates each pāramitā in succession on its respective stage.
In its ultimate stage, all virtues are fully perfected and there is nothing further to be cultivated.
What fault is there in saying that cultivation [is still required]? Answer: If one were to allow for further cultivation, [it would contradict the nature of the ultimate state].
They are not called those beyond training (aśaikṣa),
nor can it be said that all Buddhas are equal in their uninterrupted progress toward enlightenment.
Because there is a distinction between prior and subsequent,
that which is called "beyond training" (aśaikṣa) is further designated as "equanimity."
It is clear that there is no habituation in the fruit;
thus, there is no doubt regarding this meaning.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
This is because the perfect wholesome dharmas of the Buddha-fruit are neither increasing nor decreasing;
therefore, they cannot be perfumers. If they were capable of perfuming, they would not be perfect.
Consequently, there would have to be a distinction of superiority and inferiority between the Buddha-fruit attained earlier and that attained later.
As for the term "that which perfumes" (*vāsaka*),
it carries the meaning of "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).
Since it is not admitted that there can be any perfuming agent in the state of Buddhahood,
it is known that there is no further cultivation at the stage of a Buddha.
Although the preceding discussion has presented both general and specific distinctions, [the conclusion remains the same].
Within the second major section,
the explanation of cultivation is now complete;
next, the elimination of hindrances will be explained.
This is divided into two parts:
first, the clarification of the two obstacles;
second, the determination of the stages of their abandonment.
The first part further consists of four sections:
first, the explanation of the general name for the two obstacles;
second, the detailed explanation following their enumeration.
Third, the classification according to consciousness;
fourth, the manifestation of innate discrimination.
Regarding what is called the "afflictive hindrance" (kleśāvaraṇa):
"Affliction" (*kleśa*) means agitation;
"disturbance" (*upakleśa*) means confusion.
These agitate and confuse sentient beings, preventing them from escaping the ocean of suffering of birth and death.
Therefore, they are called "afflictions" (*kleśa*).
"Obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) means to cover or to conceal;
that is, these afflictions cover and conceal *nirvāṇa*, such that one cannot attain liberation.
The first is called the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
As for the second, the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
it consists of all phenomena (*dharmas*), whether contaminated or uncontaminated, conditioned or unconditioned.
This is the object of knowledge;
because it acts as an obstruction, it obstructs that object of knowledge and hinders the cognizing mind.
That which causes the mind not to comprehend its object is called the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
According to the actual reality:
The two obstacles both obstruct the two fruits.
To speak of them specifically,
the former obstructs nirvāṇa.
Subsequently, they obstruct bodhi.
Second, regarding the detailed explanation according to their enumeration:
first, the afflictions (*kleśa*) are clarified.
The following section lists those things to be known.
Within the afflictions (*kleśa*), the primary ones are clarified first,
followed by the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Regarding the "roots," there are six in total:
namely, greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, and wrong view.
This means that these six types are the roots of the secondary afflictions (upakleśa);
therefore, they receive the name "roots.
As for what is called "attachment" (rāga):
That is to say, its nature is attachment;
hatred has the nature of causing harm.
Delusion (moha) has the nature of being bewildered and obscured regarding all principles and phenomena.
Pride (māna)...
The nature of pride (*māna*) is to exalt oneself in comparison to others.
The nature of doubt (*vicikitsā*) is hesitation regarding the principles of the Truths.
As for wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*):
It has as its nature defiled wisdom that erroneously speculates upon the principles of the truths;
its nature is unwholesome,
or else it is comprised within the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta).
Therefore, they are collectively termed "evil.
Within these evil views, there are five distinctions:
first, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
To grasp at the five aggregates of clinging as "I" and "mine" is the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); *satkāya* is a Sanskrit term,
which in the vernacular [Chinese] is translated as "the view of shifting and turning."
This view grasps those five aggregates of clinging as "self" and "what belongs to self"; therefore,
it is also called the view of self and what belongs to self,
and the view of the two extremes.
This means that one adheres to either annihilationism or eternalism regarding those very [aggregates].
The intended meaning is that the view of self arises subsequently.
Grasping at the self as conceived by the view of self and other,
one regards it as either annihilated or eternal;
therefore, it is called an "extreme" (anta).
Third is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
All inverted views function in a distorted manner with respect to the objects of knowledge.
All are termed wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Fourth, the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) refers to [the attachment] toward all views and the aggregates (*skandha*) upon which they depend.
They grasp [these views] as supreme and capable of attaining purification.
The intention is this:
as for what is called "all views,"...
Because there are sixty-two and other such distinct variations,
they are called "various.
These follow the two types of divergent views according to what each has studied for themselves.
To reckon this view and the substance of the five aggregates upon which that view relies as being the supreme means for attaining purification, liberation, and transcendence,
is called the "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
The grasping at precepts and observances refers to the attachment to those precepts and observances that accord with various views, as well as to the aggregates upon which they depend,
regarding them as supreme and capable of bringing about purification.
The commentary says:
This means that the various non-Buddhists each receive their respective precepts based on their own views;
thus, the cause of the precepts arises from their views.
This is called the "precept in accordance with views.
One falsely clings to these precepts and the substance of the five aggregates upon which the precepts depend,
regarding them as the supreme means for attaining the pure fruit of nirvana.
Therefore, it is called "clinging to precepts" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
As for the subsequent secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*),
they are of the same category as the outflows (*niṣyanda*) of the root [afflictions].
Furthermore, because it is established based upon that,
it receives its name accordingly.
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
It should be understood that all these aforementioned secondary afflictions (upakleśa) belong to the category of primary afflictions (kleśapakṣya).
There are twenty distinct types of such secondary afflictions.
First is anger (*krodha*),
which has the nature of being provoked by a presently manifest, non-beneficial object.
Second is resentment (*upanāha*).
Preceded by anger,
it has the nature of harboring malice without relinquishing it and maintaining a grudge;
there are three types of concealment (*mrakṣa*).
Its nature is to conceal one's own committed offenses out of fear of losing profit and reputation.
It is preceded by anger and resentment among the four types of affliction.
Its nature is to pursue contact with violent heat and to be perverse and stubborn.
The five types of envy (*īrṣyā*) have the nature of being unable to endure the prosperity of others due to devotion to one's own fame and gain, and thus being jealous and envious.
Sixth is stinginess (*mātsarya*),
which has the nature of being attached to wealth and the Dharma, being unable to give them away, and being secretive and parsimonious.
Seventh is deception (*śāṭhya*).
Flattery (*māyā*) has the nature of hypocrisy and deceit for the sake of gaining profit and reputation while falsely manifesting virtuous qualities.
Deceit (*śāṭhya*) has the nature of employing crooked and circuitous behavior by feigning a different demeanor in order to ensnare others.
Ninth, harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*):
its nature is to lack compassion for sentient beings and to cause them injury and affliction.
Tenth, arrogance (*mada*).
The eleventh is lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), which has as its nature deep attachment to one's own prosperity and the arrogance that results from it;
it is characterized by disregard for one's own dharma and the rejection of the noble and the virtuous.
12. Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*):
having the nature of disregarding the world’s esteem and being violent and evil.
13. Restlessness (*auddhatya*).
Its nature is to cause the mind to be non-quiescent with respect to its object.
Fourteenth, torpor (*styāna*):
its nature is to cause the mind to be incapable of functioning with respect to its object.
Fifteenth, lack of faith (*āśraddhya*):
its nature is a state of mental impurity characterized by an inability to endure, take pleasure in, or desire [the truth], virtues, and capabilities.
Sixteenth, laziness (*kausīdya*).
Laziness is characterized by indolence regarding the cultivation and abandonment of wholesome and unwholesome states.
Heedlessness is characterized by a lack of restraint and self-discipline regarding defiled and purified states.
Eighteen, loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*):
its nature is the inability to clearly retain objects of focus in memory.
Nineteen, distraction (*vikṣepa*).
Its nature is to cause the mind to wander among various objects of focus.
Twenty: incorrect awareness (*asamprajanya*).
Its nature is to have a mistaken understanding regarding the object under observation.
Next, the fundamental cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are also six;
their secondary manifestations number twenty,
being the same as those of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Why is this so? The answer is: afflictions are established based upon the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*);
because they are the supported and the support, their number and so forth are equal.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"As for the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
it is either more or less according to what is appropriate."
As was explained regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*),
one should understand accordingly that their number is the same as that of the afflictions;
they are not listed separately.
Third, regarding the analysis by way of consciousness:
Question—Among the eight consciousnesses, with which consciousnesses are these afflictions associated?
Answer—First, regarding the ten fundamental [afflictions], according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*:
The eighth storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is entirely dissociated [from these].
The seventh manas-consciousness has four [afflictions] arising simultaneously:
namely, greed, delusion, pride, and the view of self.
The sixth consciousness is associated with all ten [afflictions].
The five consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth, possess only three types:
namely, greed, hatred, and delusion.
Question: Why is this so?
Answer: Because the eighth [consciousness] is comprised solely of the indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), whereas the afflictions are defiled (*kliṣṭa*).
Because their natures are different, they do not coexist.
In the seventh [consciousness], there is continuity and a constant internal grasping at a self;
because it is grasped by self-love, greed can arise.
In reality, it is not the self;
because one is deluded regarding the principle of non-self, there is ignorance.
Specifically, because the self one clings to causes the mind to become uplifted, pride arises;
one falsely conceives of that which is not the self as being the self.
Therefore, there is the view of a self.
Why is there no other [view]?
Answer: Because one loves the self, one cannot give rise to hatred.
The view of a self (ātmadṛṣṭi) certainly cannot give rise to doubt;
because the view of a self exists, there is no other extreme view (antagrāhadṛṣṭi).
This is because the essence of these five views is all wisdom (prajñā).
It is impossible for multiple wisdoms to arise simultaneously within a single moment of mind;
therefore, the seventh consciousness is associated with only four afflictions,
whereas the sixth consciousness universally permeates all three moral natures.
Because they possess superior power with respect to internal and external objects,
they are fully endowed with the ten [mental factors].
Since the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, are incapable of deliberation, they lack pride (*māna*).
Because there is no conceptual discrimination, doubt cannot arise;
because no grasping is produced, the five views do not exist.
As for the secondary afflictions:
Because this [restlessness] is exclusively defiled, it does not coexist with the eighth consciousness.
Within the seventh consciousness, there are only the "great eight," namely:
restlessness (auddhatya).
Lethargy,
lack of faith,
and indolence.
Heedlessness,
loss of mindfulness,
and distraction.
Regarding improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*),
it can coexist with all [mental factors] in the sixth consciousness.
The five sensory consciousnesses can be associated with eighty types of factors, such as lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*).
Question: Why is this so? Answer:
The meanings of the eighth and sixth [factors] are the same as explained previously;
for restlessness (*auddhatya*) and the other [seven] pervade all defiled minds.
The seventh is that when associated with defilement, eight [mental factors] arise together.
When the five consciousnesses are defiled, they can also possess eight;
for lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) are omnipresent in all unwholesome minds.
The five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, can be unwholesome;
therefore, they are capable of association.
Next, regarding the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*):
The number of mental factors associated with these various consciousnesses is the same as that of the afflictions;
therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Within the seven evolving consciousnesses..."
According to what is appropriate,
whether more or less, it is as explained in the case of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Since this treatise follows the same precedent, it will not be discussed here. Fourth, the manifestation of the co-emergent and the conceptual [afflictions]: * **Co-emergent afflictions** (*sahaja-kleśa*) are those that arise simultaneously with the object; they are innate and do not depend on prior instruction or reflection. * **Conceptual afflictions** (*vikalpa-kleśa*) are those that arise through the power of false discrimination; they depend on prior learning, reflection, or the influence of others. These two types manifest in various ways according to their respective conditions. Specifically, when the co-emergent afflictions are active, they function as a continuous, underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) that is difficult to perceive. When the conceptual afflictions are active, they manifest as overt, discursive thoughts (*paryavasthāna*) that are easily recognized. Thus, the former are subtle and pervasive, while the latter are coarse and intermittent. Together, they constitute the full range of afflictive activity within the continuum of sentient beings.
If these afflictions arise spontaneously by their own nature, without depending on the power of false teachings, false conceptualization, or false teachers,
such types are called innate (*sahaja*).
If it must arise through the power of evil friends, wrong discrimination, false teachings, and so forth,
it is called "discriminative.
Among the ten fundamental afflictions:
Greed, hatred, pride, delusion, the view of a self-identity, and the view of extremes—
these six types are common to both innate (*sahaja*) and conceptual (*vikalpita*).
As for doubt, false view, the view of grasping at views, and the view of grasping at precepts and rituals:
These four types arise solely from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*),
for they are produced only through one's own deliberate reflection under the influence of evil friends or false teachings.
Since these secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) arise based upon the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), [they are likewise so classified].
If they arise based on the fundamental innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*),
then all twenty types of derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*) that depend upon them are termed "innate.
If they arise based on the fundamental discriminative afflictions (*vikalpita-kleśa*), [they are termed "discriminative"].
The secondary afflictions that can rely upon them are all termed "discriminative.
Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"All twenty [secondary afflictions] are common to both innate and discriminative types."
Because they arise following the force of the two afflictions (*kleśa*),
the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) likewise possess both fundamental and derivative forms;
their innate (*sahaja*) and conceptual (*vikalpita*) aspects are identical to those of the afflictions.
Therefore, they are not stated separately;
although the four sections differ,
they all collectively constitute the first part, which distinguishes the hindrances.
Next, to clarify the stage of abandonment:
there are generally two types of abandoning afflictions.
The first is the abandonment of seeds.
First, it causes [the afflictions] to be forever without remainder.
Second, it merely subdues them,
causing the power of their seeds to decline so that manifest afflictions do not arise.
If one cuts off its seeds,
it is solely through untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*);
if one causes its power to decline, [it is through other means].
Both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) cognitions are attained.
However, in the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), for a bodhisattva who attains awakening instantaneously, uncontaminated cognition has not yet arisen as an actual manifestation;
consequently, they are entirely unable to sever the two obstacles.
Although one may possess faith in the principle of consciousness-only through the four powers,
one is still unable to subdue the two obstacles; therefore,
the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
Since one has not yet realized the suchness of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra-tathatā*) at this stage,
it is clearly understood that the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) has not yet been attained.
Furthermore, it says:

In this stage, although the bodhisattva has deep faith and understanding in the principle of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) by virtue of the four superior powers— namely, the power of the cause, the power of a spiritual friend, the power of mental attention, and the power of the provisions—
they have not yet realized the emptiness of the grasped object and the grasping subject.
Therefore, regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) induced by the two types of grasping,
one still lacks the power to suppress and extinguish them,
such that those two types of grasping do not arise as manifest activity (samudācāra).
Regarding the "two graspings," these are the two obstacles:
the afflictive obstacle and the cognitive obstacle.
Specifically, the seeds of these two obstacles are termed "latent tendencies" (anuśaya).
Because these seeds follow sentient beings as they transmigrate through the three realms,
they are called "concomitant" (anuvartin);
for they constantly abide within the eighth consciousness.
It is called "sleep.
Question: If it is said that in this state one does not suppress the two obstacles, to speak briefly:
Furthermore, this contradicts the three teachings.
First, since the doctrine of Consciousness-Only is self-evident,
why is it necessary for that treatise to state it again?
When a bodhisattva abides in this stage of the equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*),
although there may be some subduing of the two types of coarse manifestations,
this contradicts the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
The verse on the Bodhisattva of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) states:
"Able to extinguish all afflictions,
forever bringing them to an end without remainder."
The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are subsumed within the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*).
This contradicts the *Madhyānta-vibhāga*,
for that treatise also states:
Now, in order to distance oneself from the obstructive factors to be abandoned and to cultivate and accumulate the remedial paths,
one diligently practices the four right endeavors.
The separate cultivation of the four abandonments occurs during the stage of the provisions (*sambhāra-avasthā*).
According to these three texts,
all [of them] involve the suppression and abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Why is it that the ninth [stage] specifically mentions "not yet subdued"?
The answer is that there are differences between innate (*sahaja*) and conceptually constructed (*vikalpita*) hindrances.
Regarding those that are innate:
Within this stage, those [afflictions] arising from conceptual discrimination have not been subdued at all;
as for those [arising from innate tendencies],
there is both subduing and non-subduing.
If that which arises from one's own reflections is present,
this stage can suppress it; however,
if it arises due to a false teacher or false teachings, [it cannot].
That is, they have not yet been subdued.
Alternatively, the initial statement "not yet subdued" may be reversed;
it refers to those [afflictions] that arise from innate tendencies as well as from false teachings and the like.
Regarding the subsequent mention of "subduing," this refers to [afflictions] arising from discrimination based on one's own power and so forth;
the meaning of the *Madhyāntavibhāga* is likewise consistent with this.
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* explains that there are two meanings [regarding the cessation of afflictions].
First, regarding those arising from self-centered conceptual discrimination:
at this stage, they are entirely suppressed and thus termed "permanently exhausted."
Second, according to the power and efficacy of the Buddha-dharma, it is possible to permanently extinguish the afflictions;
this does not mean that they have already been completely exhausted at this stage.
If all delusions were actually eliminated at this stage, [it would contradict the teachings].
Why did you not attain perfect enlightenment at this very moment?
Why is it that you only attained Buddhahood after ten kalpas had passed?
Therefore, they are distinct when compared against one another.
There is no contradiction with any of the teachings.
In this stage of application (*prayoga*), one has already completed the stage of accumulation (*sambhāra*),
having fully cultivated merit and wisdom and refined the mind.
Having already attained superior power,
one is able to suppress and eliminate the two types of conceptual obstacles when entering the path of seeing; however,
the two types of innate obstacles have not yet been fully suppressed.
The seeds of both the innate and the discriminative [afflictions] remain entirely unsevered,
because true outflow-free wisdom has not yet been realized and the contemplative mind of the outflowing state still apprehends objective referents.
Because of the presence of conceptual discrimination,
it has not yet been entirely subdued and eliminated,
nor has it been completely extinguished.
The two preceding [stages] are able to suppress the afflictions through the contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*) of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Question: By what power is this contaminated wisdom able to suppress them?
Answer: As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*,
one is able to subdue the afflictions by cultivating the three types of remedial powers (*pratipakṣa-bala*).
First, one thoroughly understands the nature and faults of the afflictions,
knowing that they can give rise to karma and invite suffering and distress in both the present and future lives.
Second, one contemplates the characteristics of the objects of focus for their antidotes.
One studies and contemplates the true suchness (tathatā) manifested by the two kinds of emptiness;
third, one maintains a continuous flow of a compassionate mind through superior wholesome qualities,
cultivating the six perfections and so forth.
This serves to support the mind;
one should know that this is the preliminary path for the right view of permanent abandonment.
Next is the stage of thorough penetration.
The reality is otherwise.
Through the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one is able to exhaust the seeds of both the afflictive (*kleśa*) and cognitive (*jñeya*) obstructions (*āvaraṇa*) regarding the three realms,
thereby attaining entry into the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the characteristics of abandonment (*prahāṇa*), the Abhidharma-śāstra states:
"Question: From what is abandonment attained?"
Answer: It does not arise from the past, because that has already ceased;
it does not arise from the future.
Because it has not yet arisen,
it does not proceed from the present;
for the path and [the fruit] do not coexist.
However, it is called "abandonment" by virtue of the coarseness (*dausthulya*) of the various afflictions;
for the sake of abandoning such and such categories of coarseness,
one gives rise to such and such categories of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).
When the antidote to a particular category arises,
the corresponding category of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) is extinguished;
they are equal and identical, just as when light arises in the world, darkness is extinguished.
Because of this dissociation from the category [of defilements],
it causes future afflictions to abide in the state of non-arising;
this is called "abandonment."
Now, the difficult points shall be explained.
Both that which is severed—the coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*)—and the path that acts as its antidote are not singular;
thus it is stated again: "in this manner."
That which can counteract is in the process of arising;
that which is counteracted is in the process of ceasing;
they arise at the same time as they cease.
This is one sameness;
when cessation and arising are simultaneous,
there is again one sameness.
For this reason, it is repeatedly stated that they are "equal and equal.
The general intent is not to speak of the cessation of the three periods of time.
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
First, regarding the gate of negation (*pratiṣedha-mukha*):
it does not sever the three periods of time,
which is the same as the Abhidharma.
Regarding the subsequent explanation through words,
it is capable of severing [afflictions] of the three periods of time;
as that same treatise states:
The mind associated with right view is able to counteract [afflictions];
it possesses no latent tendencies (anuśaya) in the present life,
nor does it possess latent tendencies in the past life.
After this moment, the mind is free from latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
even in future lives, it will likewise be without latent tendencies.
Subsequently, having undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), the latent tendencies have been permanently severed.
Within the continuum of the body, all subsequent attainment minds— whether wholesome or neutral— that are comprised within the mundane state,
whether past, future, or present,
are entirely free from latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Therefore, it can be said that [the defilements] of the three periods of time are all abandoned.
This means that,
by the power of cultivating the Noble Path within the continuity of a single body from beginning to end, [they are severed].
It causes the fundamental consciousness and the others to become free from latent tendencies (anuśaya) throughout all three times;
therefore, it is called "severing the three times.
Question: Since that true path of seeing consists of only a single moment of mind...
Why does the Abhidharma repeat "thus" with respect to the path of remedy?
Answer: It is stated according to those who possess the three minds of the path of seeing;
alternatively, it may be seen as a combined statement regarding the path of cultivation and the path of remedy.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"When practitioners sever afflictions and so forth," this clearly refers to the teaching on the severance of all afflictions.
It is not only the path of seeing;
the two aspects of the path of seeing are also divided into two.
The first three moments of mind are the aspect of seeing that eliminates the afflictions to be abandoned.
This refers to all forms of *dauṣṭhulya* (corruption) categorized as weak (*mṛdu*) and so forth, which are named as listed above.
Question: Which categories of afflictions are termed "weak" and so forth?
Explanation:
What are termed "superior-grade afflictions" (adhimātra-kleśa) are here called "mild-grade" (mṛdu).
What are termed "superior-grade obstacles to the Dharma" (adhimātra-dharmāvaraṇa) are here called "medium-grade" (madhya).
The two hindrances at their lower grade are collectively termed the third.
Question: Since the first two hindrances are of the superior grade, why are they described as "mild" (soft) and "middling"?
The answer is: because the path capable of severing [the afflictions] is of a weak or middling degree,
the obstructions are designated as weak or middling according to that wisdom.
Question: According to these two obstacles, they are merely divided into upper and lower levels;
why then is a second intermediate level not established?
Answer: The middle grade is indeterminate;
it may belong to either the upper or lower grades.
Therefore, it is not treated separately.
The upper and lower [realms] are not so;
therefore, they do not mutually encompass one another.
This is just as it is stated in the sūtras, which speak only of the power of the faculties (indriya) of the upper and lower realms.
The intermediate strength is not mentioned;
the intention here is likewise.
As for the afflictions abandoned by the subsequent sixteen moments of mind:
This also has two aspects:
namely, the distinction between the grasper and the grasped, and the distinction between the higher and lower truths;
however, the number of afflictions to be abandoned remains the same without difference.
For now, we shall simply rely on the contemplation of the grasper and the grasped.
The Abhidharmasamuccaya and other treatises state:
"That is to say, beneath the Truth of Suffering, there are four kinds of mind."
First is the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
This refers to contemplating the suchness (*tathatā*) of the truth of suffering within the three realms,
thereby correctly severing the twenty-eight types of discriminative latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering within the three realms.
Explanation:

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) is possessed of ten afflictions (*kleśa*), namely the ten fundamental ones. In each of the two upper realms, the truth of suffering possesses nine [afflictions].
Because there is no hatred in the higher realms,
the three realms consist of only twenty-eight [factors].
Since this is the case for the Truth of Suffering in the three realms, [the same applies to the other truths].
The three truths of origination, cessation, and the path are each spoken of in combination with the three realms;
each of these contains twenty-eight [factors].
Taken together, this accounts for the four truths.
The one hundred and twelve types of conceptualized afflictions are eliminated by the path of seeing.
Question: Are all conceptualized [afflictions] completely severed within the true path of seeing?
Furthermore, how could there be the severance of the characteristics of conceptual afflictions?
The answer is: In principle, the characteristics of views do not sever afflictions;
rather, it is spoken of as "severance" by way of the provisional and the real.
Question: Why is there no hatred (*dveṣa*) in the higher realms?
Answer: Hatred is exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Within the two higher realms, because of the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is nothing that is unwholesome.
Next is the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*).
First the general, then the specific.
As for the general abandonment:
The innate afflictions that exist within the various consciousnesses prior to the seventh stage can still manifest; however,
from the eighth stage upward, they can be suppressed and will never again arise.
When the ten stages are fulfilled and the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests,
all innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) throughout the three realms are severed and exhausted simultaneously within a single moment.
Upon attaining perfect enlightenment,
the cognitive obscurations are gradually severed stage by stage throughout the ten bhūmis.
It is only upon reaching the Vajra-samādhi that these are finally severed and exhausted;
as for the obstacles known through the first six consciousnesses,
they never again manifest from the eighth bhūmi onward.
Because the sixth consciousness is purely uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
although the preceding five consciousnesses are not themselves uncontaminated,
they are nonetheless so by virtue of the fact that the consciousness which induces them is uncontaminated.
Because the uncontaminated [wisdom] exerts a subduing influence,
the visual and other consciousnesses likewise encounter no obstruction;
furthermore, the seventh consciousness may also arise from the eighth stage onward.
When the sixth consciousness enters into the realization of the emptiness of persons,
its seventh consciousness is still characterized by outflows (āsrava); therefore,
it acts as an obstacle to the arising [of liberation].
If one enters the contemplation of dharmas,
that seventh consciousness is the Wisdom of Equality; therefore,
they do not arise simultaneously.
Question: Why do Bodhisattvas on the ten stages not sever the seeds of those afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), but only suppress them?
Furthermore, prior to the seventh stage, they generally suppress them so that they do not arise;
do they possess such a capacity?
The answer is that the afflictive hindrances do not obstruct the ten stages;
therefore, they are not eliminated [at those stages].
This is because they obstruct nirvāṇa.
The Vajra [nature] is eternally relinquished.
Furthermore, because the power of a bodhisattva enables them to rescue sentient beings from the very first stage (bhūmi),
they remain and do not depart.
Since [afflictions] still arise even on the seventh stage,
the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"As for the obstacle of afflictions..."
From the first bhūmi upward, one is able to suppress them all at once so that they never again manifest,
just like an arhat.
By the power of intentional effort,
although it may temporarily manifest within the first seven stages, it does not do so naturally.
And this does not constitute a fault.
Furthermore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"One retains afflictions until they are exhausted."
"He realized the all-knowledge of a Buddha.
According to such passages,
it is simply that he intentionally remained [in the world], not that he was unable to subdue [the afflictions].
Question: Since it is admitted that a Bodhisattva of the seventh stage can give rise to afflictions, they should incur the fault of being defiled.
Answer: Although they do give rise to afflictions...
It is without defilement and without loss.
What constitutes its luminosity?
The answer is found in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (78), the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, and others, which state:
These bodhisattvas, within the first stage,
have definitively and thoroughly mastered the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) of all phenomena;
for this reason, [they attain this].
A bodhisattva only gives rise to afflictions when they know [the object];
it is not because of ignorance.
Therefore, this is called the characteristic of being undefiled.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Since suffering cannot arise within one's own self,
there is no fault."
When a bodhisattva gives rise to such afflictions,
they are able to sever the causes of suffering within the realm of sentient beings;
therefore, they possess immeasurable merit.
It is further said:
"Now, even the afflictions that arise in bodhisattvas still surpass the roots of virtue of all sentient beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas."
According to these teachings,
although afflictions may arise,
there is no defilement or transgression.
Next, regarding the specific abandonment:
the essence of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is not further differentiated across the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
As for the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it should be understood according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, and other such texts.
There are ten layers of obstructions,
which are severed individually at each stage within the ten stages (bhūmi),
enabling one to realize the ten suchnesses (daśatathatā).
To state it briefly now:
first is the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*).
By means of this, one is able to obstruct the noble nature of the three vehicles.
Therefore, the name "obstruction" is established.
One enters the first stage (*bhūmi*) precisely to sever this obstruction.

Question: The obstruction of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*) is established based on the seeds of the two obstructions—afflictive (*kleśa*) and cognitive (*jñeya*)—which are rooted in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Since the two obstacles are eliminated precisely upon the path of seeing,
it is clear that the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) is also severed along with them. Why,
then, is it said here that it is only in the first stage (*bhūmi*) that it is eliminated?

Answer: Although the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is eliminated by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), this path of seeing is subsumed within the initial mind of the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Here, we clarify that the ten stages eliminate the ten obstacles.
Whether [the afflictions] are hidden or manifest is not discussed;
since it is stated that they are severed at the first stage (bhūmi),
there is likewise no error.
Question: This obstruction is also established based on the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
When it is severed, the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) is eliminated, and the afflictions are also removed.

Question: Why is it said that while all ten obstacles are established based on the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is not abandoned throughout the ten stages?
Answer: Although this state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) relies upon both obstacles, it is eliminated simultaneously at the first stage.
However, the intention of the Mahāyāna is to take the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Furthermore, since followers of the two vehicles also sever afflictions (*kleśa*),
[the Mahāyāna] establishes this [definition] to distinguish itself from them.
This speaks only of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
The remaining nine obstacles are in fact established solely based upon that obstacle to the objects of knowledge.
Question: Is the innate obstacle to the objects of knowledge abandoned at the first stage (*bhūmi*)?
Answer: In reality, it can also sever them;
however, the treatises and other texts speak only of what is severed at the very beginning, referring to the severance of the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
In reality, even the mind that abides in and emerges from the first bhūmi is capable of severing those innate obstacles.
Second is the obstacle of improper conduct,
whereby one's practice suffers deficiency.
The transgressions of the three types of action are therefore called "wrong conduct," as they are able to obstruct those pure precepts.
This is termed an "obstruction.
It is a portion of the innate cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that is permanently severed upon entering the second stage (*bhūmi*).
The obstacles to be abandoned in each of the lower stages are all, one by one, portions of the innate aspect of the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Third is the obstacle of dullness,
which causes the dharmas practiced through the three types of wisdom to be lost or forgotten.
Therefore, it is called "darkness and dullness.
Furthermore, because it can obstruct the superior meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), the dhāraṇīs, and the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*) produced by those superior meditative concentrations,
it is termed an "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*).
Upon entering the third stage, one is able to abandon the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle afflictions,
because these are of the lowest degree.
Because it does not function as an object of mental attention and persists far into the background of active mental processes,
it is called "subtle."
Because this obstructs those factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), it is designated as an "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*).
It refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth among the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of the sixth consciousness.
This is because, in the past, this view of a self-identity frequently arose spontaneously along with the afflictions of the body-view (*kleśasatkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Although this view is currently designated by the name "affliction," it is not actually an affliction;
upon entering the fourth stage, one is able to eliminate it.
Fifth is the obstacle to parinirvāṇa in the lower vehicles.
The two vehicles are termed "lower" because bodhisattvas,
like them, delight in the bliss of nirvāṇa and feel aversion toward the suffering of saṃsāra.
Therefore, it is called the parinirvāṇa of the Lesser Vehicle (hīnayāna).
Because this can obstruct the path in which saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are without distinction, it is termed an "obstruction" (āvaraṇa).
It is only upon entering the fifth stage that one is able to eliminate it.
The sixth is the obstacle of the active manifestation of coarse characteristics,
which consists of clinging to both cessation and the path as being pure.
Suffering and its origin constitute defilement.
To grasp these two states of mind as being coarse and arising in subsequent stages without having ceased is called the "active manifestation of coarseness."
Because it can obstruct the path of undefiled purity,
it is termed an "obstruction.
Upon entering the sixth stage, one is able to eliminate it.
The seventh is the obstacle of the active manifestation of subtle characteristics;
although one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination,
one still perceives subtle arising and ceasing.
The subtle characteristics of arising and ceasing have not yet been stilled;
this is called "subtle active manifestation.
By means of this, one is able to obstruct the wondrous path of signlessness in the seventh stage.
Therefore, it is called an "obstruction.
It is only upon entering the seventh stage that it is eliminated.
Within the eighth stage, which is characterized by signlessness, there exists the obstruction regarding the application of effort (*prayoga*).
Characteristics such as arising and ceasing are all inconsistent with the true nature of reality;
this is termed "signlessness.
However, the wisdom of signlessness has not yet attained the capacity to function spontaneously and effortlessly.
However, it only arises through preparatory effort (*prayoga*), which is therefore termed "preparatory effort.
By means of this preparatory effort,
one is obstructed from the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-mārga*) of the eighth stage.
Therefore, it receives the name "obstruction.
Upon entering the eighth stage, one is able to permanently extinguish this obstruction regarding the lack of desire to practice the nine ways of benefiting others.
To enable sentient beings to leave suffering and attain happiness is called benefiting others;
now, one seeks only one's own benefit.
"Not delighting in guiding others" means that among the perfections for benefiting others, one does not wish to practice them.
Because of this, it can obstruct the four types of unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) within the ninth stage.
Therefore, it is called an obstruction.
Only upon entering the ninth stage is it finally eliminated.
Tenth is the obstruction of not yet having attained mastery over all phenomena.
The various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), dhāraṇīs, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), activities,
and all such meritorious qualities are collectively termed "dharmas.
Because these dharmas are not singular, they are referred to as "various" (*nānā*).
In this Dharma, being unable to exercise exclusive mastery is called "lack of sovereignty.
By virtue of this, one is able to obstruct the great dharma-knowledge and so forth within the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Therefore, they are called "obstructions.
Only upon entering the ten stages (bhūmis) can they be completely eliminated.
Although there are many different approaches above, [the essential point remains the same].
The first major section, the comprehensive analysis of the causal stage, is now concluded.
The second major section clarifies the results attained;
herein, the obstacles are first explained.
Subsequently, the manifestation of the fruit is revealed.
Although one has attained mastery over all the qualities and dharmas within the tenth stage,
there still remain residual obstructions.
It is not yet called "ultimate," because there still exist innate subtle cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as well as spontaneously arising seeds of affliction (*kleśa*).
Because they obstruct the stage of Buddhahood,
these ten stages are not called "Buddha.
When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, [one attains it].
They all suddenly sever [the obstructions] and enter the stage of the Tathāgata;
subsequently, they manifest the attainment of the fruit.
Question: When the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are fulfilled and the virtues of the ten thousand practices are complete, the auspicious causes have reached their consummation.
What is the supreme fruit?
The answer is: those two dharmas—great enlightenment (mahābodhi) and parinirvāṇa—are the fruits obtained.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"One simultaneously abandons the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
thereby becoming an Arhat and becoming a Tathāgata."
The realization of Great Nirvāṇa and Great Bodhi is their fruit.
The Tathāgata and the Arhat are distinct designations based on the meaning of Bodhi and other such factors.
It does not possess a separate substantial entity.
Now, [the text] divides nirvāṇa and so forth into two parts;
first, it explains nirvāṇa.
The meaning of bodhi and nirvāṇa will be explained later; as there are many categories of these meanings,
for now we shall rely solely on what was attained by the Buddha.
This is divided into two parts:
first, the four kinds [of emptiness] are distinguished based on *Vijñaptimātra*;
second, the three matters are elucidated based on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Regarding the four kinds:
first is the nirvana of original self-nature purity,
which refers to the principle of suchness (tathatā) regarding the characteristics of all phenomena.
Although there is adventitious defilement,
its intrinsic nature is pure and endowed with immeasurable, subtle, and wondrous virtues.
Without arising and without cessation,
it is as serene as empty space;
it is equally and universally shared by all sentient beings.
It is neither identical to nor different from all phenomena;
it is free from all marks and all conceptual discrimination;
the paths of thought are cut off and the ways of names and words are severed.
It is realized within by the true noble ones alone;
because its nature is fundamentally quiescent,
it is called nirvāṇa.
Explanation:
Its essential nature is fundamentally non-defiled;
although it serves as the basis for the sensory objects and afflictions, [it remains pure].
Yet it is not defiled;
therefore, it is called "primordially pure.
This essence is precisely the *tathatā* of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa-tathatā*) among the seven kinds of *tathatā*.
Therefore, names and characteristics are like illusions;
all phenomena are impermanent,
whereas nirvana is permanent.
Therefore, it cannot be called identical with all phenomena;
yet, because it is the true nature of all phenomena,
it cannot be called different from them.
Difference should not be the intrinsic nature of dharmas;
just as color differs from sound, and color does not have the nature of sound,
so too is its nature fundamentally quiescent.
This clarifies the name "nirvāṇa.
Perfect tranquility is the meaning of nirvāṇa.
Second is nirvāṇa with remainder.
This means that when true suchness emerges from the afflictive obscurations,
although there remains a subtle suffering because its basis has not yet been extinguished,
the obscurations are forever stilled.
Therefore it is called "nirvāṇa.
Explanation:
The body upon which one relies is termed "having a remainder of support" (sopadhiśeṣa).
The truth manifested when all afflictions within the remaining basis have been exhausted is called "the state with a remaining basis" (*sopadhiśeṣa*).
As for the statement that there is still a subtle basis of suffering,
this refers to the body of karmic maturation, which is a tainted fruit of suffering, and is termed "subtle suffering."
This is based on the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder) of the two vehicles;
it is not spoken with reference to the Buddha.
For the Tathāgata, all outflows (*āsrava*) have been entirely exhausted.
How could suffering exist?
Third is nirvana without remainder,
which means that true suchness itself transcends the suffering of birth and death.
When afflictions are exhausted and the remaining basis is extinguished, all suffering is eternally stilled;
therefore, it is called nirvana.
Fourth is non-abiding nirvana (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*).
This refers to true suchness (*tathatā*) emerging from the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
constantly supported and assisted by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and prajñā.
By this, one does not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa,
but brings benefit and happiness to sentient beings until the end of the future.
Functioning while remaining eternally quiescent is therefore called nirvāṇa.
Explanation:
Having emerged from the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one attains great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and prajñā;
this is unlike the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who delight in dwelling in nirvāṇa,
nor like ordinary beings who delight in saṃsāra.
Because both do not abide, they are called "non-abiding.
However, the substance of these four kinds is one True Suchness;
they are distinguished according to their meanings.
Now, the four meanings of the fruit of Buddhahood are all complete.
Question: Since the Tathāgata has exhausted the body that is the basis for outflows and suffering, how can it be said that he possesses these four?
Answer: It is said that there is "no remainder" (anupadhiśeṣa) because suffering and delusion have been exhausted;
it is not said that there is "with remainder" (sopadhiśeṣa) because a basis for suffering still exists.
Therefore, it can be said that the Blessed One possesses all four [nirvāṇas].
The five untainted aggregates (anāsrava-skandha) are called the non-basis of suffering.
Next, regarding the explanation of the three matters for entering nirvana,
this is based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The secret treasury is like the three dots of the letter *i*;
if they are aligned horizontally, they do not form the letter *i*,
nor do they form it if they are arranged vertically.
Just as the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara must be present for the letter *i* to be formed,
so too, if the three dots were separate, it could not be formed.
I am also like this.
The dharma of liberation is not nirvana;
the body of the Tathāgata is also not nirvana.
The Mahāprajñā is not nirvāṇa;
nor is nirvāṇa the case when these three dharmas are distinct from one another.
I now abide securely within these three dharmas.
It is for the sake of sentient beings that one is said to enter nirvana;
this is explained by the analogy of the world-character *ī*.
The wisdom that is able to realize the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and of phenomena—is called *prajñā*.
The true suchness (*tathatā*) of the two kinds of emptiness—the persons and phenomena that are realized—is called the body of the Tathāgata.
This is because wisdom realizes the principle.
To be free from all obstructive defilements and not be bound by them is called liberation.
Regarding the letter *i*:
according to the explanation in the Western regions,
in that country the two dots of the letter *i* are positioned above.
The single dot is situated below.
The lower dot symbolizes principle (li),
for it is that upon which [phenomena] depend.
The first two metaphors illustrate liberation through prajñā,
as they arise based on principle.
Why do the other three not individually constitute nirvāṇa?
The answer states that "nirvāṇa" means perfect quiescence (*parinirvāṇa*).
If it were merely *prajñā*...
If True Suchness has not yet been realized and the obscurations have not yet been liberated,
how can it be called parinirvāṇa?
If it were merely the Absolute Truth alone...
If the wisdom that realizes [nirvana] is not free from afflictions and has not severed them,
how can it be called "quiescence"?
If it were merely liberation, [it would not be true quiescence].
If the essence of liberation were merely provisional,
and both wisdom and principle were non-existent,
who could be called "perfectly tranquil"?
Therefore, these three distinct states are not called nirvāṇa.
The general meaning of this statement is that they are neither identical nor different;
only when these three dharmas exist simultaneously can it be termed entry into Great Nirvāṇa.
Wisdom is conditioned;
its principle is unconditioned.
The wisdom that realizes this principle is the reality.
Liberation is conventional;
therefore, it is not identical [to the ultimate].
This is because conditioned and unconditioned phenomena differ in being conventional and real, respectively.
Wisdom is that which realizes;
principle is that which is realized;
liberation is the freedom from bondage.
Therefore, they cannot be different.
If they were distinct,
with respect to whom could cognition be called the "realizer"?
The same principle applies to the other [two] matters accordingly.
Thus, one knows that these three things cannot be treated as separate and distinct entities.
Only in this way can it be called "entering Great Nirvana."
The meaning of *nirvāṇa* is indeed manifold;
fearing that the text would become overly prolix, I have not fully detailed it here.
Next, I shall distinguish *bodhi*.
This is divided into two parts:
first, the elucidation of bodhi;
second, the inclusion within the marks of the body.
The seeds of bodhi have existed from beginningless time;
however, they are merely obscured by the two hindrances,
which prevents them from arising.
Subduing and severing [the afflictions] over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and practicing through the ten stages (*bhūmi*),
one reaches the stage of the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*), where both obstacles are entirely exhausted.
Wisdom arises from seeds;
this is called the attainment of bodhi.
This very bodhi, when associated with the mental factors (caitta), consists of four types in total.
Therefore, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts state:
"The first is the mental complex associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom;
that is to say, this mental complex is free from all conceptual discrimination."
Its objects and modes of activity are subtle and difficult to know;
it is neither forgetful nor deluded,
and its perception of all objective phenomena is free from all defilements.
Its pure and perfect qualities are continuous and uninterrupted,
extending to the furthest reaches of the future,
like a great round mirror manifesting all manner of forms and images.
Explanation:
Simultaneous with wisdom,
the mental factors are not unitary.
These are collectively termed the "mental factors" (*caitta*).
The grasping at a self and so forth, as well as the subject and object of apprehension—
all such things are non-existent and are called "free from conceptual construction" (*nirvikalpa*).
Because both the subjective faculty of cognition and the objective object of cognition are equally ungraspable,
it is called "subtle";
yet, with respect to its objects, it is neither deluded nor obscured.
Therefore, it is called "not deluded.
To be present before all things without forgetting them is called "non-forgetfulness."
The permanent exhaustion of outflows (āsrava) is called freedom from defilement (vairāgya).
Being unmixed, it is termed pure;
being free from faults, it is called clean (śuddha).
Pure virtues are fully perfected;
thus, one attains the name "Perfect" (Vairocana).
In all places, one is able to manifest bodies and lands.
It is called "uninterrupted" because it manifests in a long-lasting continuity without ceasing; therefore,
it is termed "unbroken."
Just as various images arise by relying upon a large, bright mirror,
so now, the reflections of the bodies and lands arise in dependence upon this wisdom.
The Dharma is made clear through its reliance on this analogy.
Therefore, it is called the Perfect Mirror Wisdom.
Second is the mental state associated with the Wisdom of Equality:
this mental state contemplates all phenomena and all sentient beings—both self and others—as entirely equal.
Great compassion and the other [virtues] are constantly in union with it;
they form a single-flavored continuity that extends to the end of the future.
Explanation.
The rational essence of suchness is called equality.
Wisdom that takes this principle as its object is called the wisdom of equality.
Furthermore, in the former state of an ordinary person, one clings to a self.
Self and others are originally unequal;
now that my grasping at a self has perished, I contemplate self and others as equal,
and thus it is called "equanimity."
It is called "one flavor" because it is without change or transformation;
it is called "continuous" because it arises without interruption.
Third is the mental state associated with the wisdom of wondrous observation.
This refers to this mental state which skillfully contemplates the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena,
proceeding without obstruction;
it encompasses and contemplates immeasurable gateways of dhāraṇī and samādhi, as well as the precious jewels of merit that they generate.
Within the assemblies of the Mahāyāna, they are able to manifest infinite varieties of activity and have attained mastery over all,
raining down a great rain of jewels.
It severs all doubts and causes all sentient beings to obtain benefit and happiness.
Explanation.
The functioning of the spirit is versatile beyond measure; it is termed "subtle.
To universally take all objects as its conditions is called "observation."
The dharmas such as the six perfections are called "precious jewels.
Because they arise from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they are termed "generated.
This refers to the mental state associated with the fourth wisdom, the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
That is to say, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings,
this mental state universally manifests various transformations of the three karmas throughout the ten directions,
accomplishing the deeds that ought to be performed through the power of its original vows.
Explanation:
The transformation of the three types of action and so forth are the activities to be performed;
because wisdom can accomplish these, it is called "Accomplishing What Is To Be Done" (Kṛtyānuṣṭhāna).
Question: Are these four wisdoms identical in substance to consciousness, or are they not?
Answer: They correspond respectively to those [consciousnesses], namely the eighth, the seventh, the sixth, and the first five consciousnesses.
The essence is not identical to consciousness,
because the king and his ministers are distinct;
consciousness serves as their king.
Because wisdom is that which is attained.
Question: For what reason do the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, and other treatises all state that one transforms those eight consciousnesses to obtain the four wisdoms?
Answer: Within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, there are two explanations.
Although a single wisdom is not consciousness,
it nevertheless evolves in dependence upon consciousness,
because consciousness is the primary factor.
It is said that they are attained through the transformation of consciousness.
Second, in the state with outflows, wisdom is weak and consciousness is strong;
in the state without outflows, wisdom is strong and consciousness is weak.
In order to encourage sentient beings to rely on wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandon consciousness (*vijñāna*),
it is taught that the eight consciousnesses are transformed to obtain the four wisdoms.
In reality, however, it is not that consciousness itself becomes wisdom.
Question: Since untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is powerful, why is consciousness still required?
Furthermore, by what means is it clarified that the Buddha-fruit possesses consciousness?
Answer: Generally speaking, what are called mental factors (caitta) must necessarily depend upon the mind-king (cittarāja).
If that consciousness did not exist, upon what would wisdom (jñāna) rely for its establishment?
Furthermore, according to the *Tathāgataguṇajñānācintyaviṣayāvatāranirdeśa-sūtra*:
"The Tathāgata’s stainless consciousness is the pure, untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*),
liberated from all obstacles."
It is associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.
According to this scriptural passage,
how could it be that the Buddha lacks consciousness?
Question: Among these four wisdoms, how many pertain to both cause and fruit, and how many are exclusively fruit?
Answer: The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is attained only upon the completion of the task and the attainment of Buddhahood; thus, it is exclusively fruit.
The wondrous contemplation of equality is attained in stages within the first bhūmi and so forth;
the fruit of Buddhahood is then fully perfected.
The term "question" (*praśna*) refers to the categories [of inquiry].
Regarding the category of the four wisdoms:
how many types are there?
Answer: Each one is definitively composed of twenty-two [factors].
The twenty-second [category] consists of the five universal mental factors and the five object-specific mental factors.
There are eleven wholesome [mental factors],
which together with the mind-king constitute twenty-two.
What are the names and meanings of these twenty-two dharmas?
Answer: As for the five universal [mental factors], their substance pervades the three realms, the three natures, and all consciousnesses;
therefore, they are called "universal."
What are these five?
First, it causes the mind and mental factors to come into contact with their respective objects;
therefore, it is called "contact" (sparśa).
Second, it is called *manasikāra* (attention) because it can awaken the seeds of the mind that are to arise,
drawing them forth toward their objects.
Third, it is called sensation (*vedanā*) because it is capable of experiencing objects that are favorable, unfavorable, or neutral.
Fourth, it is capable of establishing boundaries regarding objects and grasping their images.
Therefore, it is called "perception" (saṃjñā).
Fifth, because it enables the mind to produce wholesome, unwholesome, and other [states],
it is called "volition" (cetanā).
Regarding the term "object-specific" (viṣaya-viniyata):
the objects subdued by these [mental factors] are not one;
they take various distinct objects as their conditions.
Therefore, they are called "object-specific" (viṣaya-viniyata). What are these five?
First, the aspiration toward an object that is desired is called *chanda* (desire).
Second, conviction (*adhimokṣa*) is the confirmation of a determined object;
third, mindfulness (*smṛti*) is the clear recollection of a previously experienced object;
fourth, concentration (*samādhi*) is the focused attention upon an object of observation.
Fifth, the discernment of the object under investigation is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
Regarding the term "wholesome" (*kuśala*) and so forth:
it is called wholesome because it is conducive to benefit in this world and in future worlds.
What are the eleven?
First, that which is able, within the true and pure virtues of the Three Jewels and the Four Noble Truths,
to possess deep patience, aspiration, and a pure mind— this is called faith (*śraddhā*).
Second, honoring and revering the virtuous and good is called *hrī* (shame).
Third, despising and rejecting the violent and evil is called *apatrāpya* (dread of blame).
Fourth, because one does not become attached to the three realms and so forth, it is called non-attachment (*alobha*).
Fifth, because one does not give rise to anger toward suffering and such things, it is called non-hatred (*adveṣa*).
Sixth, because one clearly understands both principle and phenomena, it is called non-delusion (*amoha*).
Seventh, because one diligently cultivates wholesome deeds and diligently abandons unwholesome dharmas with courageous decisiveness, it is called diligence (*vīrya*).
Eighth, because one is far removed from coarse heaviness and the body and mind are well-adjusted, it is called pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
Ninth, guarding against evil and cultivating good is called non-negligence (*apramāda*).
Tenth, causing the mind to abide in equanimity and straightforwardness without effort is called equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Eleventh, not harming sentient beings is called non-harming (*avihiṃsā*).
Question: It is beyond doubt that ordinary beings and others possess universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*) and so forth;
however, how is it that the fruit of Buddhahood also possesses these?
Answer: That which is universally associated with all minds is called "pervasive" (sarvatraga).
Therefore, it must exist in a Buddha. If it were absent in a Buddha, [it would contradict the definition].
What is meant by "universal" (sarvatraga)?
The eleven wholesome mental factors, such as faith and so forth, are necessarily present [in all wholesome minds].
Since the Buddha is exclusively wholesome, he possesses faith and the other factors.
Because the Tathāgata constantly delights in realizing the object of contemplation, he possesses desire (*chanda*);
because he perpetually maintains a firm mental impression of the object of contemplation,
he possesses resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
Because one constantly maintains clear mindfulness of objects previously experienced,
mindfulness is likewise present;
the Blessed One has no state of non-concentrated mind.
Therefore, one also attains concentration;
because one constantly discriminates all phenomena,
one attains wisdom.
Question: The body of the Tathāgata possesses boundless virtues;
for what reason are only twenty-two mentioned?
Answer: These twenty-two encompass all the conditioned merits of a Buddha, leaving none unaccounted for.
Based upon these twenty-two factors,
various designations are established;
there is no separate essence existing apart from these.
Regarding the mutual inclusion of the two bodies:
first, the bodies are distinguished;
subsequently, their mutual inclusion is clarified.
The Buddha-body is not uniform, but consists of three types.
The first is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*),
which refers to the true and pure Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of all Tathāgatas.
It is endowed with infinite, truly pure merits;
it is the equal, ultimate nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
This very nature is the basis upon which the dharmas of great merit rely.
It is called the *dharmakāya*,
because the meaning of "body" (*kāya*) is that of a basis.
Furthermore, this *dharmakāya* possesses only reality, permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Free from all defilements,
it is the basis of all virtues and the unconditioned merit.
It lacks the characteristics and functions that differentiate mind, form, and so forth;
furthermore, it is perfectly self-benefiting because it is quiescent,
peaceful, blissful, and devoid of activity.
It also benefits others concurrently,
acting as a dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya) to cause all sentient beings to obtain benefit and happiness.
He dwells in the land of the dharma-nature (dharmatā-bhūmi).
Although there is no distinction in essence between this body and its land,
they differ in terms of their attributes and characteristics as they belong to the Buddha and the Dharma respectively.
It is called "land" (kṣetra) according to its nature,
because it is that which serves as the basis;
it is called "Buddha" in terms of its characteristics.
Because this is that which serves as the basis of reliance,
and because both this body and its environment are not material form (*rūpa*),
it is impossible to speak of their dimensions or magnitude.
However, the extent of these phenomena according to their specific characteristics is boundless,
for they are like space, which pervades all things;
this is because the phenomena that are so pervaded are themselves immeasurable.
That which is able to pervade all phenomena is also called "immeasurable.
Regarding the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*), there are two types:
first, the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*).
This refers to the boundless, true merits and pure form-bodies accumulated by all Tathāgatas over three incalculable eons,
which continue in an unchanging, serene state throughout the limits of the future.
He constantly enjoys the vast dharma-pleasure for his own sake;
because he experiences pleasure for himself,
it is called "self-enjoyment."
Furthermore, because they seek only their own benefit and do not preach the Dharma for others,
they dwell in lands of self-indulgence.
Because the causes and conditions of the merits for one's own benefit cultivated in the past have been fulfilled,
from the moment of initial enlightenment until the end of the future,
these realms will continuously transform into purely pure Buddha-lands.
It is circular and boundless,
adorned with various jewels,
and the body of self-enjoyment constantly dwells therein.
As is the extent of the pure land,
so too is the extent of the body;
the various faculties such as the eyes, as well as each of the primary and secondary marks, are individually infinite.
Because it is produced by the drawing forth of infinite roots of goodness,
and because merit and wisdom are not material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*),
their dimensions— whether large or small— cannot be described.
Based on the realized principle and the supporting body,
it may also be said to pervade all places.
Second, the Body of Enjoyment for Others.
This refers to the Tathāgatas manifesting sublime bodies to appear before the assembly of bodhisattvas of the ten stages,
displaying supernatural powers and preaching the Dharma.
It decisively cuts through the web of doubts of sentient beings and causes them to enjoy the bliss of the Mahāyāna Dharma;
this is called the "Enjoyment for Others" (parasaṃbhoga).
Furthermore, it possesses the merit of transformative marks that benefit others, such as infinite forms resembling those of physical matter and mind;
moreover, it is solely for the benefit of others.
Because they manifest for the sake of others,
they dwell in their own lands;
this is due to the accomplishment of the causes and conditions for a pure, untainted Buddha-field through the practice of benefiting others in the past.
According to what is appropriate for Bodhisattvas dwelling on the ten stages,
they transform it into a pure land—
whether small or large, superior or inferior.
The bodies of enjoyment for others (parasaṃbhogakāya) abide depending upon these [transformations],
and the dimensions of these supporting bodies are likewise without fixed limit.
Combining these two— the enjoyment bodies of oneself and others—
they are collectively termed the "enjoyment body" (saṃbhogakāya).
Third is the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya).
This refers to the Tathāgatas manifesting immeasurable transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) that accord with the various types of beings;
for the sake of bodhisattvas who have not yet ascended the stages, as well as those of the two vehicles and ordinary worldlings,
they manifest supernatural powers and preach the Dharma in accordance with their respective capacities.
That which manifests through skillful means to cause each [being] to obtain various beneficial and blissful matters is called the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body).
It possesses exclusively the merit of transformative marks— such as form and mind that appear boundlessly— which bring benefit and happiness to others;
it is comprised solely of benefiting others,
because it manifests for the sake of benefiting others.
They dwell in lands of transformation.
These are accomplished through the causes and conditions of their past cultivation of the altruistic, untainted pure and impure Buddha-lands;
they manifest as Buddha-lands according to what is appropriate for sentient beings who have not yet ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*).
Whether pure or defiled, small or large,
they undergo successive transformations;
the Buddha’s transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) abides in reliance upon them.
The dimensions of the bodies upon which they depend are likewise not fixed.
Second, regarding their mutual inclusion:
how do these three bodies correspond with the five dharmas?
Answer: True Suchness alone subsumes the Dharmakāya.

Why is this so? According to the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Vasubandhu’s *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and other such works, it is stated as follows:
The Dharma-body is without arising and without cessation,
because its essence, which is True Suchness (tathatā), is itself without arising or cessation. Furthermore,
it is stated in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, and other such works.
The Dharma-body of the Buddhas is shared by all Buddhas;
it is only the principle of True Suchness (tathatā) that is shared by all Buddhas, whereas the others are not so.
If that is so, why does the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* state that by transforming the ālayavijñāna one attains the dharmakāya?
The answer is: because the eighth consciousness contains the seeds of the two obstacles;
thus, it is by means of being able to extinguish these seeds of the two obstacles [that transformation occurs].
This clearly reveals the Dharmakāya.
Based on this, it is said that one transforms the ālayavijñāna to attain [the Dharmakāya];
however, in reality, consciousness itself is not the Dharmakāya.
Second, among the four wisdoms such as the mirror-like wisdom, the constant and pervasive form-body arising from the mirror-like wisdom—
which is the true merit— is subsumed under self-enjoyment. How is this known?
The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states that the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* also says:
By transforming the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), one attains the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*).
Therefore, it is known that the substance of the Enjoyment Body consists generally of the actual form and mind of the mental states of the four wisdoms.
Third, the Buddha-body manifested by the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) subsumes the Body for Others' Enjoyment (*para-saṃbhoga-kāya*).
The various types of physical forms manifested by the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna) comprise the nirmāṇakāya.
All the form and mind belonging to these two bodies are merely semblances and not real.
Why is this so? It is because these are all manifested as skillful means for the sake of transforming others;
therefore, it cannot be said that true wisdom constitutes their essence.
Now, the stages, practices, principles, and matters of the One Vehicle are profound and vast;
were it not for one of perfect virtue,
what else could possibly be said?
For this reason, even those on the great stage of Equal Enlightenment remain as deluded as the moon obscured by clouds;
those in the minor position of the Śrāvakas still have their jewel-like nature shrouded by the garment.
Their wisdom remains thus.
How much more so for those who are deaf to the drum!
It is simply that waves arise because of the sea,
and light shines because of the sun.
Since things are thus,
how could the Dharma not exist?
Therefore, relying on the words of the Sage, it has been compiled into successive stages.
I bequeath this to those of like inclination,
hoping that their cultivation will gain momentum;
yet this aspiration remains unfulfilled.
Therefore, the *Udānavarga* (Verse Summary) says:
"Relying upon the words of the noble ones,
one discerns the stages and practices of the Mahāyāna."
May all sentient beings attain the state of perfect enlightenment and abide therein forever.

This concludes the first fascicle of the *Mahāyāna-avatāra-krama* (The Stages of Entering the Path of the Mahāyāna). Indeed, this chapter uniquely opens the door and window for escaping from suffering.
This correctly demonstrates the stages for entering the Path;
it is the eyes and feet of the practitioner,
and the very core of that which can express the truth.
Therefore, although I have harbored the wish to carve printing blocks and publish [this work] to propagate it far and wide over these past years,
my daily meals have often been limited to a single bowl,
and I have had absolutely nothing to set aside beyond my three robes.
Consequently, while I have long harbored the aspiration to circulate this work,
I had not yet reached the stage of carving the woodblocks;
fortunately, I was graced by the generous assistance of the Ichijōin family.
Suddenly, after many years, the fundamental aspiration for compassion has been fulfilled;
this is entirely due to the power of invisible resonance.
I pray that you will deign to lend an ear and cast a glance.
It is merely that by reading the texts and understanding their meaning,
one will swiftly bring to fruition the seeds of the nature of universal benefit, thereby attaining the fruit of Bodhi.

On a day in the third month of the eighth year of Bun’ei (1271), the patron, the śramaṇa Eison of Saidai-ji, made this vow solely for the sake of the long endurance of the True Dharma and the benefit of sentient beings.
